claims.claim: Eldridge notes the back of the book gives further information on the Kesh in a traditional ethnographic form.
claims.source: Cat Eldridge, review of Always Coming Home, A Green Man Review
claims.quote: contains additional information about the Kesh in a traditional ethnographic

claims.claim: Eldridge advises that Always Coming Home is best read in very small pieces rather than continuously.
claims.source: Cat Eldridge, review of Always Coming Home, A Green Man Review

claims.claim: Nathanael Bonnell describes Always Coming Home as not a single story but a collection of texts.
claims.source: Nathanael Bonnell, review of Always Coming Home, New Maps (Winter 2021), republished Resilience.org 16 Feb 2023
claims.quote: not a single story but a collection of texts

claims.claim: Bonnell lists the document types the book collects, including short plays, songs, a chapter of a novel and personal accounts.
claims.source: Nathanael Bonnell, New Maps / Resilience.org, 16 Feb 2023
claims.quote: short plays, songs, a chapter of a novel, personal accounts

claims.claim: Bonnell notes the present-day culture survives in the Kesh record only in stray fragments of folklore.
claims.source: Nathanael Bonnell, New Maps / Resilience.org, 16 Feb 2023
claims.quote: remembered only in stray fragments of folklore

claims.claim: Bonnell reports Le Guin stages a dialogue between herself as narrator and a Kesh village archivist.
claims.source: Nathanael Bonnell, New Maps / Resilience.org, 16 Feb 2023
claims.quote: a dialogue between herself-as-narrator and a Kesh village archivist

claims.claim: Bonnell reports Le Guin opens by asking the reader to bear with some unfamiliar terms until they come clear.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, quoted by Nathanael Bonnell, New Maps / Resilience.org, 16 Feb 2023

claims.claim: Oliver Tearle calls the Omelas narrator an uncertain narrator, as distinct from an unreliable narrator.
claims.source: Dr Oliver Tearle (Loughborough University), Interesting Literature, February 2021
claims.quote: as distinct from an unreliable narrator

claims.claim: Tearle notes the narrator confesses to lacking detailed knowledge of the laws and rules of Omelas.
claims.source: Dr Oliver Tearle, Interesting Literature, February 2021
claims.quote: lacking detailed knowledge of the laws and rules of Omelas

claims.claim: Tearle summarises that the city is characterised by the institutions it lacks: no King and no slaves.
claims.source: Dr Oliver Tearle, Interesting Literature, February 2021
claims.quote: They have no King, and do not keep slaves

claims.claim: Tearle notes the description denies the city a stock exchange and advertisements.
claims.source: Dr Oliver Tearle, Interesting Literature, February 2021
claims.quote: they have no stock exchange and no advertisements around the city

claims.claim: Sarah Wyman argues the long lines of the first paragraph mimic the festival parade the words describe.
claims.source: Sarah Wyman, professor of English at SUNY-New Paltz, analysis at Literary Ladies Guide
claims.quote: long lines of the first paragraph mimic the festival parade

claims.claim: Wyman identifies a chiastic sound echo in the opening description of Omelas.
claims.quote: echoing the sonic features with a chiastic

claims.claim: Wyman quotes the narrator interrupting the description of the city to ask how one is to tell about joy.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, quoted by Sarah Wyman, Literary Ladies Guide
claims.quote: How is one to tell about joy?

claims.claim: Wyman reads the narrator as divesting herself of authority and responsibility for defining Omelas.
claims.quote: divest herself of authority and responsibility for defining Omelas

verdicts.trueWording: the “back of the book” contains additional information about the Kesh in a traditional ethnographic form
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200, live URL, browser UA). Quote is verbatim in the review body; byline 'Cat Eldridge' present on page. Every limb (back of book / further info on Kesh / traditional ethnographic form) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: it can be — and definitely should be — read in very small pieces
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. 'rather than continuously' is supported on the same page: 'It took me months to read Always Coming Home because I read a wee bit at a time in the evenings.'

verdicts.trueWording: Always Coming Home is not a single story but a collection of texts
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200). Quote verbatim in review body; Bonnell byline and New Maps Winter 2021 / 16 Feb 2023 ed. note both present on page.

verdicts.trueWording: They include short plays, songs, a chapter of a novel, personal accounts
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; page continues 'pen-and-ink sketches, proverbs, and types of art that we have no word for', so the claim's 'including' is accurate rather than exhaustive.

verdicts.trueWording: today is remembered only in stray fragments of folklore
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Full sentence: 'The culture that you or I would find if we visited the environs of the Napa Valley today is remembered only in stray fragments of folklore, as “the Red Brick People”...' — the remembering frame on the page is the Kesh's.

verdicts.trueWording: she orchestrates a dialogue between herself-as-narrator and a Kesh village archivist
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; page adds she accuses the archivist's world of being a utopia. 'Le Guin stages' matches 'she orchestrates'.

verdicts.trueWording: In the beginning Le Guin asks the reader's forbearance to “bear with some unfamiliar terms [until it] will all be made clear at last”
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. 'opens by' = 'In the beginning'; 'until they come clear' = the bracketed continuation plus 'it does come clear in a most satisfying way'.

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator is what we might call an ‘uncertain narrator’ (as distinct from an unreliable narrator)
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200). Quote verbatim in the Analysis section; byline 'By Dr Oliver Tearle (Loughborough University)' and date 2021-02-20 confirmed on page.

verdicts.trueWording: Although the narrator confesses to lacking detailed knowledge of the laws and rules of Omelas
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, in the plot-summary section as the claim states; page continues 'they suspect there are relatively few.'

verdicts.trueWording: They have no King, and do not keep slaves
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the summary. The claim's framing 'characterised by the institutions it lacks' is the claim's own compression, but the page's summary paragraph is itself a catalogue of lacks (no King, no slaves, no stock exchange, no advertisements, no secret police), so the limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: they have no stock exchange and no advertisements around the city
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; page prefaces it with 'Consumerist culture is unknown to the people of the city'.

verdicts.trueWording: The breathless, long lines of the first paragraph mimic the festival parade the words describe
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200). Quote verbatim; page states 'This analysis is contributed by Sarah Wyman, professor of English at SUNY-New Paltz.'

verdicts.trueWording: echoing the sonic features with a chiastic au-gr / gr-a flip
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, in the same first-paragraph discussion: 'Le Guin alliterates the sounds of the words: “mauve and grey, grave…”' — so 'opening description of Omelas' holds.

verdicts.trueWording: How is one to tell about joy? How to describe the citizens of Omelas?
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, quoted by Wyman under 'A jarring wake-up call': the narrator 'makes two moves that jerk us out of traditional fairy tale mode' and 'problematizes her own tale-telling goal', supporting the 'interrupting the description' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: The narrative voice's move to divest herself of authority and responsibility for defining Omelas
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; page continues 'further implicates the reader in completing the construction of this anti-utopia.'
